Sep 25, 2026, 9:16 PM ET
Seattle Mariners relief pitcher Andres Munoz (knee) was placed on the 15-day Injured List on Friday, Ryan Divish reports. Munoz hasn't pitched since Sunday, and now goes to the shelf due to right knee inflammation. His inconsistent 2026 season will now come to an end with a few games left in the regular season. He'll finish the season with a 4.24 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, and an 89/24 K/BB ratio with 28 saves across 57.2 innings of work. The expectation is that Jose A. Ferrer and Seranthony Dominguez will work in save situations over the final few days of the regular season. Fantasy managers should expect Munoz to be back in the closer role and fully healthy for the start of next season.--Andy Webb
Source: Ryan Divish

Xavier Edwards Still Out for Marlins


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 6:07 PM ET
Miami Marlins middle infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) remains out of the starting nine for Friday's series opener at home against the division-rival Atlanta Braves, per MLB.com. Jared Serna will make another start at second base for the Fish and will hit in the nine-hole against Braves left-hander Ray Kerr. This will be Edwards' fifth straight missed game after he aggravated a left-thumb injury last Saturday against the San Diego Padres. The Marlins have not rushed the 27-year-old back after being eliminated from playoff contention. At this point, he only has two more chances to return before the end of the regular season on Saturday and Sunday against Atlanta. The switch-hitting middle infielder was having a second straight solid season for the Fish this year, slashing .280/.360/.371 with a .730 OPS, a career-high six home runs, 52 RBI, 21 stolen bases, and 61 runs scored across 142 games and 595 plate appearances. You are not going to get any power from Edwards, but he remains useful for his speed and contact-oriented approach at the dish in fantasy leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Luis Arraez Out on Friday, Report "Not a Great One"


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 6:01 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies infielder Luis Arraez (ankle) is out of the team's starting lineup on Friday against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays, and the report on his ankle injury from Thursday night is "not a great one," interim manager Don Mattingly told Scott Lauber of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Mattingly did not give a grade on the sprain, and the Phillies have not decided on an injured-list placement, which would take Arraez out until at least Oct. 5, or around Game 3 of the divisional round. X-rays on Arraez's left ankle came back negative on Thursday night, but his sprained ankle is still stiff and sore, which is why he will not play on Friday. Bryson Stott is at second base and batting fifth on Friday, with Edmundo Sosa at third base and hitting ninth against Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta. The Phillies would obviously love to avoid putting the 29-year-old All-Star on the IL, but if he cannot play at all this weekend, they might have no choice. The four-time All-Star and three-time batting champion has hit only .278 (49-for-176) in his 46 games with the Phillies this year after being traded from the San Francisco Giants in early August, but he is still the league's leading hitter at .310 overall. Not having Arraez available next week for the start of the playoffs (if the Phillies qualify) would be a big loss for Philadelphia.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Philadelphia Inquirer - Scott Lauber
Zyhir Hope Appears To Be Future Fantasy Star


Brian Buckey




Sep 25, 2026, 1:46 PM ET
Detroit Tigers new top outfield prospect Zyhir Hope showed off plenty of promise with Double-A Erie following his trade from the Dodgers in the Tarik Skubal deal. Hope was the headline piece coming back to Detroit after dealing away their ace, and he proved his potential with a massive minor-league season at the Double-A level between the Dodgers and Tigers. The 21-year-old left-handed hitter combined to hit .287 with 29 homers and 111 RBI to go with 86 runs scored and 26 stolen bases. Hope has a 50-grade hit tool with 60-grade power and 55-grade speed. The future is bright for Hope, and he could make his debut with the Tigers in 2027. Expect the five-category skills Hope has shown in the minors to translate to the big leagues, making him a great target for fantasy managers as soon as next season.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Caden Hunter Looks Like Future Fantasy Ace


Brian Buckey




Sep 25, 2026, 1:38 PM ET
Baltimore Orioles pitching prospect Caden Hunter turned in a dominant 2026 minor-league season between three levels. Finishing up at Double-A Chesapeake in his age-22 season, Hunter combined to pitch to a 5-3 record with a 2.01 ERA and 1.06 WHIP with 151 strikeouts in 103 innings pitched. In his first professional season out of USC, Hunter dominated to hold opposing hitters to a .171 batting average. The 6-foot-2, 205-pound left-hander is the No. 4 overall prospect of the Orioles and boasts a 60-grade fastball and a 55-grade slider and changeup combination with a 45-grade curveball. Hunter looks like a future fantasy star with the size and skills to be a dominant force on the mound with the Orioles in the future. Look for more of Hunter in the minors in 2027, with the potential to make his MLB debut as soon as next season.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 1:27 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers pitching prospect Christian Zazueta combined between High-A Great Lakes and Double-A Tulsa to have a stellar age-21 minor-league season in 2026. Zazueta's overall numbers ended up very good, with a combined 6-4 record, 3.65 ERA, and 0.97 WHIP with 144 strikeouts in 103 2/3 innings. The 6-foot-3 right-hander limited opposing batters to a .214 batting average. He is the No. 5 prospect in the Dodgers' system with a 60-grade fastball and changeup combination with a 50-grade secondary pitch in his slider. Zazueta shows very good control and looks to have all the tools to be a future fantasy-relevant pitcher. It could be a few years before Zazueta makes his MLB debut, but he looks like a great dynasty-league addition in the near term.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller

Connelly Early to Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 1:26 PM ET
Washington Nationals left-hander Connelly Early (elbow) threw 40 pitches across 1 2/3 innings with Triple-A Rochester on Sept. 20 and will come off the 60-day injured list to make one more start this season this weekend against the division-rival New York Mets, according to MLB.com. Early landed on the injured list on July 1 and was moved to the 60-day IL on Aug. 22 due to inflammation in his left elbow. It will be his first start with the Nationals after the team acquired him from the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline in early August. In his 17 starts (91 2/3 innings pitched) for the BoSox this year in his second season in the big leagues, Early went 7-5 with a 3.44 ERA (4.60 FIP) and 1.25 WHIP with 93 strikeouts and 34 walks. He had a 2.33 ERA and 1.09 WHIP in a smaller sample size of only four starts in his first taste of the big leagues near the end of the 2025 campaign. Early, a fifth-rounder from Virginia in 2023, is one of the more intriguing young lefty arms in baseball, but he will be far too risky in starting fantasy lineups with championships on the line this weekend against New York after his long injury layoff. UPDATE: Early will make his Nationals debut on Saturday.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 25, 2026, 1:19 PM ET
Detroit Tigers catcher prospect Josue Briceno overcame wrist surgery and battled a late ankle injury in what was an injury-plagued age 22 minor league season. Briceno combined between four minor-league levels in 2026 to combine for a .250 batting average with nine homers and 29 RBI and 23 runs in 42 total games. Briceno played 15 games at Triple-A Toledo and hit just .196 in a very small sample size. He hit .297 in 17 games at Double-A Erie prior to his call up to Toledo. Briceno is the No. 4 prospect of the Tigers and has a 50-grade hit tool with 60-grade power. The catcher position is in good shape in Detroit with All-Star Dillon Dingler and Eduardo Valencia. Briceno is a power bat with limited speed that could potentially shift to first base or find a spot at DH if needed, but he is still a big part of the future plans for Tigers brass and could make a 2027 debut.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 1:10 PM ET
Washington Nationals shortstop prospect Devin Fitz-Gerald split his minor-league season between two levels but finished with nice overall numbers in his age-21 season. Between High-A Wilmington and Double-A Harrisburg, Fitz-Gerald combined to hit .251 with 20 homers and 67 RBI, along with 15 stolen bases and 78 runs scored. The switch-hitter was originally drafted by the Texas Rangers and came to the Nationals organization in the MacKenzie Gore trade. Fitz-Gerald is the No. 5 prospect for the Nationals and has a 50-grade hit tool with 50-grade power and 45-grade speed. Fitz-Gerald looks like he could be an impact player for the Nationals, but Washington does have another elite shortstop prospect in Seaver King, so Fitz-Gerald's future could involve another infield position.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller

Tampa Bay Rays first base prospect Xavier Isaac had a good minor league season at age 22 and closed it off well with a good stint at Triple-A Durham. Called up to Durham from Double-A Montgomery on August 25, Isaac played 18 games with the Durham Bulls down the stretch. He finished that stint with three homers and eight RBI in 59 at bats with a .271 batting average and 11 runs scored. Altogether between Montgomery and Durham, Isaac combined to hit .258 with 27 homers and 79 RBI to go with 20 stolen bases and 88 runs scored. Isaac is the No. 18 prospect in the Rays system and looks like he could be ready for a role on the 2027 Rays team. Isaac appears to be a promising talent with 60-grade power, but just a 35-grade hit tool. He could be a good homer and RBI threat but leave something to be desired in the batting average category.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller

Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) is out of the starting lineup yet again for Game 1 of a doubleheader on Friday against the visiting Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park, according to MLB.com. On Thursday night, a week after he was hit on the knuckle between the ring finger and pinkie on his right hand, Contreras expressed concern about his availability for the start of the wild-card series in the American League next week. "I mean, it's really concerning," said Contreras. "But at the same time, I'm putting all my effort -- and everything I can do, I'm doing it. I don't know what else to say. I'm working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better. But I haven't been able to swing the last two days." If the Red Sox do not have Contreras, their best power hitter this season, it will be a big blow to their chances of making a deep postseason run. Before injuries struck this month, Contreras was having a career year in his first season with the team, slashing .276/.387/.518 with 27 home runs and 81 RBI in 129 games played. Andruw Monasterio is starting at first base for Game 1 on Friday and is hitting eighth against Cubs right-hander Clay Holmes.--Keith Hernandez

Alex Bregman Returns as DH on Friday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 11:33 AM ET
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (face) is back in the starting lineup on Friday and will serve as the designated hitter and bat third in Game 1 of a doubleheader at Fenway Park against the Boston Red Sox, per MLB.com. Bregman is back for the first time since he suffered multiple facial fractures on Sunday against the Cincinnati Reds when he was hit by a foul ball in the on-deck circle. Bregman did not need surgery, though, and he has been cleared to hit only in the series opener against his former team after the swelling around his left eye went down. The 32-year-old will now look to get his timing back down in the final weekend series of the regular season before the Cubs start a wild-card series in the playoffs next week. Bregman has bounced back in 2026 in his first year in Chicago with 26 home runs and 89 RBI while slashing .262/.352/.452 in 153 games. He also hit .296 (34-for-115) in 28 games in August and is currently hitting .295 (18-for-61) in 18 games in September. The Cubs are hoping Bregman can stay hot heading into the postseason next week.--Keith Hernandez

Overall, the 28-year-old has been one of the better power hitters and run producers at the catcher position in MLB this year. Dingler's strikeout rate is manageable at 22.9%, and he's posted solid barrel (10.0%) and hard-hit (42.7%) rates. Riley has been a bit better in the second half of the season, hitting .248 with 10 home runs across 233 plate appearances since the All-Star break. Contreras has not played since September 17 after being hit by a pitch on his right hand. Philadelphia Phillies infielder Luis Arraez (ankle) suffered a sprained left ankle in Thursday's game against the Milwaukee Brewers, and the Phillies say that he will be evaluated further, according to Lochlahn March of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Arraez tried to avoid being tagged on a ground ball in the sixth inning at Citizens Bank Park and should now be considered day-to-day until we have more details. Braves fans can breathe a sigh of relief that they did not lose Acuna just before the start of the playoffs next week, and they will be hoping he can carry over his hot hitting in September. Luzardo said the session went well. The Phillies could look to have Luzardo throw a simulated game this weekend to face live hitters, and he remains very much in play to return to the starting rotation for the start of the postseason next week in the wild-card series. The Phillies must first get into the postseason, as they entered Thursday tied with the Chicago Cubs for the final wild-card spot in the National League, with the Arizona Diamondbacks on their tails at three games behind with four left to play. Luzardo will be eligible to come off the 15-day injured list for the regular-season finale on Sunday, but he almost certainly won't be an option to pitch in that game as the Phillies look to save him for the playoffs. Getting the 28-year-old southpaw back for next week is the team's top priority after he went 14-5 with a career-best 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, and 221:52 K:BB in 178 2/3 innings across 29 starts in his second year with the organization.--Keith Hernandez

Luis Arráez sufrió un esguince en el tobillo izquierdo y los Phillies esperan conocer su disponibilidad para el resto de la campaña.
Las alarmas están encendidas en los Philadelphia Phillies en uno de los tramos más complicados del calendario. El segunda base venezolano, Luis Arráez, abandonó el terreno de juego este jueves ante los Milwaukee Brewers tras sufrir un esguince en el tobillo izquierdo, una lesión que llega cuando el equipo pelea por asegurar su lugar en los playoffs.
No se trata de una ausencia menor. Arráez lidera la Liga Nacional con promedio de .310 y representa una pieza central en una ofensiva que necesita contacto, turnos largos y presencia constante en circulación. Su estatus para los últimos juegos de la temporada regular y una eventual Serie de Comodines todavía no está definido.
El primer parte médico del equipo es un tanto alentador. Las radiografías descartaron una posible fractura, pero el equipo aún debe determinar el grado del esguince y cuánto puede limitarlo al correr, defender la segunda base y ejecutar su juego de contacto.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Luis Arráez cambio MLB 2026: destinos del venezolano
¿Cómo se lesionó Luis Arráez con los Phillies?
Le lesión de Arráez se produjo en la sexta entrada ante Milwaukee, con el encuentro igualado 1-1. Arráez conectó un rodado al campocorto Cooper Pratt, quien realizó un tiro desviado hacia la primera base. Jake Bauers tuvo que salir de la almohadilla para recibir la pelota e intentar el toque.
Arráez se desplazó hacia su derecha para esquivar a Bauers, pero apoyó mal el pie y se torció el tobillo izquierdo. El venezolano cayó de inmediato sobre el terreno, se tomó la zona afectada y requirió atención del personal médico. Posteriormente salió del campo con ayuda, sin poder avanzar con normalidad hacia la cueva.
La jugada también terminó con un out por salirse de la línea de carrera, una decisión que generó protesta desde el dugout de Philadelphia. El resultado, sin embargo, quedó en segundo plano. La preocupación pasó a ser la condición física de uno de los bateadores más difíciles de retirar en las Grandes Ligas.
¿Qué dijeron los Phillies sobre la lesión de Arráez?
Los Phillies confirmaron un esguince en el tobillo izquierdo y anunciaron una evaluación adicional durante este viernes para poder tener una visión más completa de su lesión.
El mánager Don Mattingly evitó adelantar un pronóstico sobre el tiempo de recuperación. “Espero que pueda jugar, pero veremos”, señaló tras el partido. También explicó que el cuerpo médico revisaría al venezolano este viernes para conocer su respuesta al tratamiento y evaluar su movilidad.
Mattingly dejó claro que el equipo no cuenta todavía con una fecha de regreso. El diagnóstico de esguince abre un margen amplio, porque la gravedad depende del daño en los ligamentos, la inflamación y la capacidad del jugador para apoyar el pie sin dolor. Philadelphia entra en horas decisivas y no puede planificar con certeza la disponibilidad de Arráez.
¿Cómo puede afectar Luis Arráez a los playoffs de Philadelphia?
La lesión amenaza con alterar la identidad ofensiva de los Phillies. Arráez no depende del poder para impactar un juego. Su valor aparece en la frecuencia con la que pone la pelota en juego, evita los ponches y crea oportunidades para los bateadores de fuerza que vienen detrás en el orden.
Philadelphia lo adquirió desde San Francisco en la fecha límite de cambios con la intención de sumar un bate de élite para el cierre de la campaña. Su promedio de .310 lo mantiene al frente de la Liga Nacional y lo coloca en la pelea por otro título de bateo. Perderlo, incluso por pocos juegos, reduce la calidad del lineup en una etapa donde cada turno puede definir una clasificación o una serie corta.
La situación adquiere más peso porque la posible Serie de Comodines comenzaría la próxima semana. El calendario ofrece poco margen para recuperar estabilidad, especialmente en una lesión de tobillo que afecta los arranques, los cambios de dirección y la defensa en el cuadro.
Edmundo Sosa entró en reemplazo de Arráez durante el juego ante Milwaukee, pero los Phillies podrían necesitar más ajustes en el infield si el venezolano no responde bien en los próximos días. Una ausencia prolongada obligaría al club a redistribuir posiciones y a cubrir un vacío complicado en la parte alta o media del orden.
Philadelphia conserva alternativas para seguir adelante, pero ninguna replica el perfil de Arráez. El venezolano aporta una habilidad que gana valor en octubre: poner la pelota en juego bajo presión. Por ahora, los Phillies celebran que no exista fractura, aunque esperan una noticia todavía más importante: que el esguince no lo saque de los juegos que pueden definir su temporada.

The Philadelphia Phillies’ lineup has looked completely different since the addition of second baseman Luis Arraez.
While his production hasn’t been as prolific with the Phillies as it was with the San Francisco Giants, having him as protection for Bryce Harper as the cleanup hitter has enabled the Philadelphia star to take his performance to another level.
The contact-first approach that Arraez brings is something the rest of the team bought into. In August, the Phillies had one of the best offenses in the MLB, improving their on-base percentage and coming up with timely hits.
However, Philadelphia looks like it could be without Arraez for the time being after he suffered a lower leg injury in the series finale against the Milwaukee Brewers. With him, the Phillies were placed last among the lineups of playoff contenders by Stephen J. Nesbitt and Chad Jennings of The Athletic (subscription required); without him, they are solidified in that spot.
Where does Phillies lineup rank among playoff contenders?
They placed the team 13th, and it is hard to argue with that placement based on the numbers in 2026. There are a lot of big names in the lineup, but not much production.
Entering the final series of the regular season, there are only two healthy Phillies players who have a wRC+ that is above the league average: Harper, with a team-high 135, and designated hitter Kyle Schwarber, with a 130.
Arraez was third with a 110, and for a lineup that has been so underwhelming for large chunks of the season, losing him creates a major void in the lineup. Right now, the most consistent hitter beyond that duo is probably Alec Bohm, who got off to a historically poor start but has been excellent in the second half.
He has a .312/.379/.445 slash line in 243 plate appearances and is batting over .300 for the second straight month.
Phillies need supporting cast to step up
Will players on the team wake up and turn things around in October? On paper, this is a star-studded group, loaded with All-Stars such as shortstop Trea Turner, catcher J.T. Realmuto and outfielder Brandon Marsh.
Unfortunately, the first two are in the midst of the least productive seasons of their respective careers, and Marsh has been arguably the worst hitter in baseball for nearly three months. Philadelphia desperately needs them, along with Bryson Stott, to catch fire once again as they did in August.
This team has proven capable of getting hot and producing at a high level. But the odds are certainly stacked against them heading into the postseason, especially with Arraez potentially being sidelined.

Luis Arraez suffered an ankle injury on Thursday night against the Milwaukee Brewers and was on the ground in pain afterward.
He exited the game, and it was revealed that his X-rays were negative and that he has an ankle sprain. With the postseason starting on Tuesday and the Phillies fighting for a spot, his status is unclear. While speaking to reporters, interim manager Don Mattingly revealed he is unsure what Arraez's status is moving forward, but he is hopeful he will return.
"I'm hopeful that he's going to play, but we'll see," Mattingly said to reporters after the game, per 97.5 The Fanatic's Colin Newby. "We'll see where it goes."
Arraez was the Phillies' big acquisition at the trade deadline. He is having a career year defensively and has been an elite hitter for his entire career. The Phillies moved Alec Bohm to first base, Bryce Harper to right field and Bryson Stott to third base to accommodate Arraez, but now they are at risk of missing the postseason. The typical recovery time for an ankle sprain would indicate that he will at least miss the Wild Card Series, but the team will further evaluate him on Friday, per Mattingly.
The Phillies still have a two-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks for the final Wild Card spot, but without Arraez, things are not looking great. Arraez's batting average has taken a hit since he joined the Phillies, as he is only hitting .278 with a .678 OPS. However, he is still on pace to win his fourth career batting title.
Losing him for the final series could cost the Phillies a postseason spot, and not having him for the Wild Card Series could have an extremely negative impact on their offense. He has 21 RBIs in 46 games with the Phillies and has a .778 OPS this season with runners in scoring position.

The Phillies have turned baseball’s oldest lineup blueprint upside down, and the runs are following, writes Jared Diamond for The Wall Street Journal.
Since reshaping the batting order, Philadelphia has raised its scoring from 4.39 to 4.67 runs per game, jumping from 16th to ninth in MLB.
For generations, the formula barely changed: a high-contact table-setter hit near the top and the biggest power bat hit in the middle.
The Phillies have flipped the script.
Kyle Schwarber, one of baseball’s most feared home-run hitters and also one of its most frequent strikeout victims, now leads off.
Batting cleanup — the spot long reserved for sluggers like Lou Gehrig and Joe DiMaggio — is Luis Arraez, a three-time batting champion with little home-run power who hits behind Bryce Harper.
With the Giants, before Philadelphia acquired him at the trade deadline, Arraez typically batted first or second.
Even manager Don Mattingly acknowledged how strange the alignment would have looked during his playing days in the 1980s and 1990s.
“Things are changing,” Mattingly said.
Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski said that in an earlier era, a hitter with Arraez’s profile would have been penciled into one of the first two spots almost automatically.
Instead, Philadelphia wants his bat in play with runners aboard, where his .349 career average with runners in scoring position can do the most damage.
The logic is rather than forcing hitters into traditional roles, build the lineup around what each one does best.
As Dombrowski put it, “It does just tell you how the game has changed.”
Read more about how the Phillies are challenging 125 years of batting-order convention and why their upside-down approach is producing more runs in The Wall Street Journal.

Brewers record their first 100-win season with victory over Phillies
The Milwaukee Brewers reached 100 wins for the first time, and Jackson Chourio hit his 25th homer to lift them to a 5-1 victory over Philadelphia on Thursday night that slowed the Phillies’ playoff push.
The Phillies needed a win to at least have a shot at clinching their fifth straight trip to the playoffs. They instead can try again to clinch for the third straight game on Friday against Tampa Bay.
Philadelphia played without NL batting leader Luis Arraez after he came off with a sprained left ankle after he tried to avoid a tag at first base.
Milwaukee reached one more milestone to go with its National League Central title and a first-round postseason bye. The Brewers are the first team this year to reach 100 wins and are trying to hold off the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers for the No. 1 seed in the NL playoffs. Their previous high was 97 wins last year.
Brewers fans crowded the seats behind the dugout and held “100” signs as players left the field.
Bryce Harper tied the game 1-1 with an RBI single in the third.
Jake Bauers hit the tie-breaking single off José Alvarado (5-4) in the eighth inning, and Cooper Pratt and Joey Ortiz added run-scoring singles in the inning for a 4-1 lead. Chourio hit a solo shot in the ninth.
JoJo Romero (3-3) got the win and Antonio Senzatela earned his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter had another terrific outing in a second-half rebound that should see him play a role in the postseason in the rotation or out of the bullpen. He allowed Sam Frelick’s RBI double in the second and finished with eight strikeouts and three walks in six innings.
The rookie right-hander was demoted to the minors in June after a 12-4 loss to Miami left him with eight losses in nine decisions and a 7.06 ERA. Since his July 31 recalled has a 3.65 ERA in 11 starts with 62 strikeouts to 23 walks.
Philadelphia got more good pitching news earlier in the day when All-Star lefty Jesús Luzardo said he has recovered enough from left shoulder inflammation that he should be able to pitch next week in the playoffs.
Up next
Milwaukee tunes up for the playoffs with a three-game homestand against St. Louis.

Brewers take down Phillies for franchise's first 100-win season
(Photo credit: Bill Streicher)
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run Thursday for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with their 5-1 win over the hosting Philadelphia Phillies.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5 and added a double, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame. Chourio, who pinch-hit for designated hitter William Contreras, led off the frame with a walk off Jose Alvarado (5-4) and stole second.
Gary Sanchez singled deep to left field to put runners on the corners, and after Alvarado got Luis Lara to line out to shallow center, Cooper Pratt (2-for-3) welcomed Chase Shugart with another hit up the middle to give the Brewers a two-run lead. Joey Ortiz added a two-out hit, a blooper to shallow center that allowed Sanchez to score from second.
Chourio added a solo home run, his 25th blast of the season, in the ninth.
Five Brewers pitchers held the Phillies (87-72) to just four hits. JoJo Romero (3-3) allowed one hit in 1 1/3 innings against St. Louis, who Milwaukee acquired him from last month. Romero picked up his second win with the Brewers since coming off the injured list (appendectomy) earlier this month.
Antonio Senzatela relieved Romero, allowing a walk over the final 1 2/3 innings to earn his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter held the Brewers to just one run over six innings. The rookie allowed five hits and three walks while matching a season-high eight strikeouts. His only blemish came in the second, when Sal Frelick doubled home Sanchez.
Kyle Schwarber (2-for-4) and Bryce Harper (2-for-4) combined to get all four of the Phillies hits. Harper's third-inning single scored Schwarber, who led off the frame with a double off Brewers starter Shane Drohan. Philadelphia managed just one hit, a Schwarber single in the seventh, against the Brewers bullpen.
Besides losing the game, the Phillies may also have lost infielder Luis Arraez, who reportedly sprained an ankle trying to avoid a tag on a groundout in the sixth inning.
With the win, Milwaukee can officially clinch home-field advantage throughout the postseason should the Los Angeles Dodgers lose Thursday night to the visiting San Diego Padres.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.
--Field Level Media

Contrary to popular opinion, the free agent market doesn’t consist of only one player. Yes, superstar starter Tarik Skubal will grab headlines since there’s nobody close. But while it may be seen as a one-man show, there are some other decent starters and useful position players. Here’s our top 30.

But it’s a weaker free agent field, and the Phillies reportedly offered $200M over seven years last winter. They should have infield openings with Luis Arraez and Alec Bohm also free agents.
3. Randy Arozarena, OF: He timed his career year well, joining AL MVP Yordan Alvarez as the only players to post a 125 wRC+ every month, via MLB Network. Seattle needs Arozarena, whose clutch gene surfaced in the 2020 postseason.

item.content:encoded:
El béisbol tiene una forma particular de escribir sus historias más bonitas: a veces, la pelea más emocionante no es entre rivales de distintas naciones ni de distintas generaciones, sino entre dos compatriotas que se persiguen en la cima. Eso es exactamente lo que está pasando en la Liga Nacional, donde Gabriel Moreno acaba de conectar su jonrón número 16 de la temporada para elevar su promedio de bateo a .312 y empatarse nada menos que con Luis Arráez en el liderato ofensivo del circuito. Dos venezolanos. Un solo trono. Y toda una temporada por delante para decidir quién se lo queda.
El golpe que lo cambió todo
Que un receptor lidere el departamento de bateo en las Grandes Ligas ya es, de entrada, una rareza que merece detenerse a contemplar. La posición de careta es, históricamente, la más exigente del cuadro: el desgaste físico, los turnos al bate interrumpidos por los cambios de entrada y la carga defensiva hacen que los números ofensivos de los receptores suelan quedarse por debajo de los del resto de la alineación. Por eso, cada vez que un catcher aparece peleando el título de bateo, la historia lo anota.
Moreno no solo aparece en esa conversación: la encabeza. Su cuadrangular número 16 no fue únicamente otro punto en el marcador, sino el empujón que lo colocó al nivel de Arráez, uno de los bateadores de contacto más consistentes del juego moderno. Que un jonrón haya sido el vehículo para alcanzar ese liderato dice mucho sobre la temporada completa que está teniendo el careta venezolano: no es un especialista de un solo recurso, sino un bateador que combina contacto y poder de manera que pocos en su posición pueden presumir.
Arráez, el obstáculo más difícil
Alcanzar a Luis Arráez en cualquier lista de bateo es mérito suficiente para encabezar una conversación. El también venezolano lleva años siendo uno de los porcentajes de contacto más altos de las Grandes Ligas, con una filosofía de bateo que parece diseñada específicamente para desesperar a los lanzadores: pocas ponchadas, muchos hits, un swing que rara vez regala outs.
Que ambos estén empatados a estas alturas de la temporada convierte cada turno al bate de los dos en un evento. Cuando Arráez conecta un hit, Moreno necesita responder. Cuando Moreno eleva su average, Arráez tiene que sostener el ritmo. Es el tipo de duelo que le da textura a una temporada larga y que los fanáticos del béisbol de verdad saben apreciar: no hay un villano ni un héroe forzado, solo dos peloteros extraordinarios empujando el uno al otro hacia lo mejor de sí mismos.
Por qué este duelo importa más allá de Venezuela
Es inevitable —y completamente válido— celebrar que el liderato de bateo de la Liga Nacional tenga acento venezolano de lado a lado. El béisbol de ese país ha producido generaciones de peloteros que han marcado el juego, y ver a dos de sus representantes actuales disputarse una corona individual en las Mayores es un recordatorio de la profundidad de ese semillero.
Pero el duelo Moreno-Arráez trasciende la bandera. Habla de dos estilos de juego distintos convergiendo en el mismo número: el receptor de poder que batea para average, y el especialista en contacto que no regala nada. Es una discusión táctica, histórica y estética al mismo tiempo.
- Gabriel Moreno demuestra que los receptores pueden ser fuerzas ofensivas de primer nivel, no solo guardianes del pitcheo.
- Luis Arráez sigue siendo uno de los argumentos más sólidos a favor del bateo de contacto en una era dominada por el poder y las ponchadas.
- La Liga Nacional tiene, en este duelo, uno de sus relatos más atractivos de la temporada.
¿Quién se queda con la corona?
Esa es la pregunta que vale la pena hacerse ahora mismo, con la temporada todavía en curso y los números tan apretados que cualquier racha —o cualquier caída— puede inclinar la balanza. El título de bateo no se decide en un jonrón ni en una semana brillante: se construye turno a turno, serie a serie, durante meses.
Lo que sí está claro es que mientras Moreno y Arráez sigan en esta pelea, la Liga Nacional tiene un argumento de primer orden para mantener los ojos puestos en ella. Y el béisbol venezolano, una razón más para sentirse orgulloso de lo que sus peloteros están haciendo en la cima del juego. La corona es de uno solo, pero el mérito, por ahora, es de los dos.

Well, I jumped the gun by a year. Last year, I got excited that the Homerless Qualifier Club might be reopening. Nick Allen was playing every day for the Braves, and Nick Allen’s approach to impacting the baseball is sort of like Atticus Finch’s approach to parenting: It’s composed almost entirely of occasional, gentle nudges in the right direction. If Allen could just get enough plate appearances, I figured, he’d qualify for the batting title without a single home run to his name, making him just the second new member since 2012. The problem was that Allen didn’t just lack punch; he couldn’t get on base at all. The Braves batted him last and pinch-hit for him every chance they got, then gave his spot to waiver wire pickup Ha-Seong Kim. Allen never homered, but he ended up 86 plate appearances short of qualifying. This year is different. This year it’s in the bag. Chandler Simpson has already qualified for the batting title, and he is about to finish the season without a single home run.
As was the case for Allen, the reason that the Homerless Qualifier Club has been closed for business for so long is that it’s really hard for a regular baseball player to be playable without any power whatsoever. Allen’s a defensive specialist whose game has never been built around the home run ball, but he still needs some base level of power to keep his offense from sinking the entire profile. Think of your favorite contact hitter – Luis Arraez, Steven Kwan, Nico Hoerner – these guys are much better at avoiding strikeouts than Allen, and they still hit the ball hard enough to rack up a bunch of doubles and at least a handful of home runs a year. Meager though it is, if that power production were to disappear, their offense would simply be too much of a deficit to overcome. They’d stop getting enough plate appearances to qualify for the batting title. That’s why the pipeline has dried up.
This season, Allen has just 161 plate appearances with the Astros, but he’s betrayed us to the tune of a whopping three home runs. Stretch that over 500 plate appearances and he’s nearly in double digits. My point is that although these are extreme examples of contact hitters, they still have plenty in common with the rest of the league. They are still looking to drive the ball, at the very least, over the infield. Simpson may as well be playing a different sport.
Simpson has an ISO of .050, the lowest among qualifiers. In fact, his career ISO+ is the 16th lowest of all time among non-pitchers. (In case you’re curious, our database also lists 132 pitchers who had a higher career ISO+, including John Smoltz. If you work for Fox and Smoltzy ends up calling a Rays game, please make sure he learns this information.) Simpson has six triples this season, and his 16 doubles rank eighth from the bottom among qualifiers. His average and 90th-percentile exit velocities are both second from the bottom. His hard-hit rate is less than half of Nick Allen’s. Nick Allen’s!
Simpson hasn’t recorded a barrel all season. In fact, over 1,041 recorded batted ball events in the majors and the minors, he’s never once been credited with a barrel. Over that time, he’s been credited with 155 hard-hit balls, but not a single one of them was hit at the right launch angle to qualify as a barrel. This year, across nearly 600 plate appearances, he’s only reached the wall on the fly twice. It’s not unusual for him to go more than a week without hitting the ball 300 feet in the air; before the All-Star break, he had a stretch that lasted more than two weeks.
That doesn’t happen by accident. Simpson doesn’t want to hit the ball a long way. Hitting the ball far means hitting it in the air. The longest ball he hit this season was a 355-foot double. Of the 24 longest balls he has hit this season, it’s one of just two that actually turned into a base hit. The other 22 ended up like this.
It’s not just that they were caught; they were cans of corn. This season, 222 different players have put the ball in play at least 250 times. Pete Crow-Armstrong leads them all with 64 base hits on fly balls. Although he ranks fourth in baseball with 531 balls in play, Simpson is dead last with just three base hits on fly balls. That’s a rate of 0.6%. The next-lowest rate belongs to Luis Rengifo, and it’s more than three times higher than Simpson’s. Simpson swings so softly that a fly ball is to him what a popup is to every other hitter: an automatic out. He’s batting just .042 on fly balls, and again, everyone else on the list at least doubles that mark (and all but five triple it). The gap is even larger if you look at wOBA. You know how some hitters, when they’re talking about their goal to hit a line drive over the shortstop, will tell you that home runs are accidents? That’s the way Simpson feels about any ball he hits with a launch angle over 25 degrees.
I don’t mean to say that Simpson is incapable of hitting the ball hard. He wants to hit the ball hard. When the Rays drafted him, Simpson was initially reluctant to add muscle in the weight room out of fear that it would hurt his speed. The team worked with him to find the right combination. “I came in very light, and they told me I needed to lift and I needed to get stronger,” he told our Matt Martell on Wednesday, “so those balls that I can hit at a certain exit velocity can get through the holes and a defender can’t get to them.”
All the same, he doesn’t hit home runs in batting practice either, not necessarily because he can’t, but because he’s working on spraying line drives all over the field. “You don’t appreciate it until you see it every day,” Rays manager Kevin Cash told The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal last year. “There is no intent to play the long-ball game.” Matt also asked Simpson whether, now that the Rays have clinched the division, he might go for a home run just for the pleasure of wrecking the premise of this article. “Go for a homer?” he replied. “No, no, no, no.” “I’m sure there are times he wants to pull the ball in the air for a homer,” starter Drew Rasmussen told MLB.com. “And who doesn’t, right? Hitting homers is cool. But, no, he knows exactly who he is.”
If you go to Simpson’s Baseball Savant page and click the Random Video button over and over and over again, as I did on Tuesday, you’ll start to focus on his legs. He has a very simple leg kick, but that’s the only pre-pitch movement going on at all. He effectively has no stride and no load. His swing is more rotational than linear, but only because it’s not linear at all. He looks like he doesn’t get into his legs at all. He treats them the way other hitters treat their head. He just wants them to be still and quiet so they don’t get in the way of the work his arms are doing. He’s effectively shortening up his swing by cutting out his lower half altogether, and somehow, it works. He’s got the third-highest squared-up rate in baseball. He looks like he’d gladly hit while sitting in a chair if the rules allowed it.
This is obviously something of an exaggeration. When asked about it Wednesday, Simpson said, “I’m definitely in my lower half when I swing. The foundation of the swing is the ground. You have to use the ground to be able to adjust. So I use the ground for adjustability, for sure. I look like that, but I definitely have to use my legs to create strength for those line drives that can get through holes and groundballs, to stay in my approach, because if I don’t have my legs then I don’t have anything.”
This focus on using the ground for adjustability is clearly visible. The only time Simpson’s legs ever really get going is if he realizes mid-pitch that he’ll be able to lay into one, at which point he’ll get some push going from his back leg. The truth is that we don’t really know how far Simpson is capable of hitting the baseball because we’ve never seen him try. In case you’re wondering, while I was using the Random Video tool, I got curious what would happen if I clicked the Home Run button. The answer: The Random Video tool just disappears from your browser altogether, like it’s censuring you for your cheek. Leave it to Baseball Savant to find a way to make a passive-aggressive website. I actually asked someone who works there if the box was supposed to function that way.
At least they weren’t passive aggressive.
Conversely, I also don’t think we should necessarily think about Simpson the way we think about other contact hitters, because his swing is so different from theirs, too. Let me show you what I mean. Below are Statcast’s wireframe models of the swings of both Arraez and Simpson. I picked Arraez because Simpson has voiced his admiration for his game. “I use his drills in my hitting regimen,” he told Rosenthal last year. On Wednesday, Simpson explained to Matt that he’s more focused on Arraez’s approach: “Really just make sure I’m finishing my swing with my head down on contact, make sure I’m trying to stay inside the ball. Make sure I’m staying low line drives in the cage, not rolling over balls.”
Knowing all that, the differences between the two swings are jarring. First, look at the back foot. Arraez’s is pushing off hard enough that when he transfers his weight forward, the momentum pulls his back foot off the ground and toward the pitcher. Simpson’s back foot doesn’t move.
Now look at the front leg. Arraez is pushing off his front leg hard. The force pushes his heel off the ground. At the moment of contact, his front leg and his torso are in perfect alignment so that he can transfer the energy it generates up the kinetic chain. At the moment of contact, Simpson’s torso is still almost completely vertical. It’s not getting any of that energy. Arraez’s front foot is planted firmly, whereas Simpson’s rotates outward, leaking power.
Lastly, look at the shoulders. When Arraez’s swing gets going, you can tell because his back shoulder is driving forward toward the ball. When Simpson’s gets going, you can tell because his front shoulder is pulling back away from it. On some level, that’s the difference between a linear swing and a rotational swing, but remember who we’re talking about here. Arraez is the most contact-oriented player in today’s game by a mile, but next to Simpson’s, his swing looks like it belongs to a power hitter.
My point in taking you through all these differences is not to denigrate Simpson’s swing, but to emphasize that it’s designed to do something else entirely (which is why MLB.com, to the chagrin of English speakers everywhere, keeps using the phrase “most unique” to describe him). Frankly, I think it’s a testament to his athleticism that he hits the ball as hard as he does while putting less of his body into it than any batter in the game. In the same way that I have no idea how hard Simpson could hit the ball if he focused on that goal, I have no idea whether he could do what Arraez does. Although he’s learning from Arraez, his swing is still different on a very fundamental level, and it’s designed to get him on base in a fundamentally different way.
When Arraez squares the ball up according to the Statcast definition, he has a 30% line drive rate. That’s actually not all that high a number; Kwan leads the league at 38%. Simpson is down at 25%. That’s because 61% of his squared-up balls are grounders, the second-highest mark in the game. You’ve heard plenty of players talk about their goal being to hit a line drive right over the head of the shortstop or the second baseman. Simpson says his goal is lower, “Trying to stay low line drive, hard groundballs.”
Simpson gets to first base faster than anyone else in the game. He leads the AL in steals (46) and bunt hits (14) and the majors in infield hits (40). In fact, since Sports Info Solutions started tracking infield hits in 2002, only three players have ever put up more in a season than Simpson’s current mark of 40: Ichiro Suzuki (who did it in seven different seasons and got a nice plaque to show for it), Norichika Aoki in 2013, and Luis Castillo in 2006. Simpson has the highest groundball rate and lowest fly ball rate in the game. SIS, which uses a different methodology from Statcast, credits him with the lowest hard-hit rate – nearly three points below Steven Kwan in second place – and the highest medium-hit rate in the game. The important thing is that what Simpson is doing is working.
Simpson won a college batting title with a .433 mark as a junior at Georgia Tech. He started this season strong, batting .407 through his first 16 games, before he fell into an ugly 54-game slump; from April 15 through June 19, he hit just .215. However, he has batted .352 across his 79 games since then, bringing his overall average up to .309, seven points behind Yordan Alvarez in the AL race. If he completes the comeback, he’ll be the first player since Buster Posey to win a batting title in both college and the majors. Simpson’s approach of putting the ball either on the ground or just over the infield gives him a 95 wRC+. Combine it with all that baserunning value and his much-improved defense, and he is up to 2.5 WAR on the season.
I imagine that some people will read this and wonder whether Simpson isn’t just today’s version of Billy Hamilton. That’s perfectly understandable, but Simpson’s approach is different even from Hamilton’s. Hamilton hit 24 career home runs, all of them over the fence. He never qualified for the batting title with fewer than four homers. His career-long batted ball traveled 417 feet, 52 feet farther than Simpson’s longest. His strikeout rate was nearly triple Simpson’s, and his fly ball rate was nearly 15% higher. He never had half as many infield hits as Simpson has this year. He also never ran a wRC+ above 79 (except during a 13-game cup of coffee in 2013).
Right now, it looks like Simpson will be able to keep on racking up homerless seasons until either his speed or his contact skills start to decline, but I’m curious to see what will happen over time. He’s still in just his second year in the majors, and I don’t think it’s out of the question that he might slowly work toward a more fluid swing that makes more use of his strength. That’s not to say that he’d fundamentally change his approach, but that as he improves, he might see the upside in trying to drive the ball for extra bases more often. After all, as you remember from spring training, he is definitely capable of hitting a home run over the fence.
However, Simpson said Wednesday that he’s never had any pressure to adjust his launch angle. “I feel like all the coaches in my career have been very understanding and know what my game is,” he told Matt. “They haven’t really tried to change that much. Maybe they’ve tried to get me to tap into a little bit more power in the sense of hitting the ball harder so they can get through holes through the infield, things like that, but not really lifting the ball.” We just need him to hold off for another week.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
Former Minnesota Twins president of baseball and business operations Derek Falvey “mutually parted ways” last spring and one of the underlying storylines of this season has been where he would end up. Taking the season to evaluate the landscape, we may have finally found our answer as The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon reported on Wednesday that Falvey will be joining the New York Mets front office under lead executive David Sterns.
At first glance, this looks like a perfect landing spot for Falvey. While we don’t know the exact reason why Falvey abruptly resigned in February, a good bet was that he was tired of the tightening purse strings from the Pohlad family when they slashed the team’s payroll in 2023 and 2024 before he orchestrated a fire sale ahead of the 2025 trade deadline. The Mets won’t have that problem as Steve Cohen is one of baseball’s most free-spending owners West of Los Angeles, but it may not have been Falvey’s biggest issue.
Instead, more money could be an even bigger problem for Falvey and while his role is undefined, there’s enough evidence to suggest that he could put the Mets in a deeper hole as he begins his next chapter.
Derek Falvey’s biggest problem with the Twins wasn’t a lack of money
The Twins hired Falvey in 2017 as a way to reboot their franchise. Terry Ryan was one of the greatest general managers in team history during their rise in the 2000s, but upon his return in 2011, his methods had gotten old and stale, resulting in what former Twins chairman Jim Pohlad called a “total system failure.”
For a team that had traditionally looked within the organization to hire managers and front office personnel, plucking Falvey from the Cleveland Guardians felt like a massive victory. The Guardians had done more with less throughout the 2010s, including a trip to the World Series in 2016, and his knack for developing pitching also convinced the Twins to bring him aboard as the executive vice president and chief baseball officer.
Falvey’s tenure came with some immediate hits, hiring manager Rocco Baldelli and signing Nelson Cruz as a free agent to spark the “Bomba Squad” team that won 101 games and set an MLB record with 307 home runs in 2019. He also signed Max Kepler and Jorge Polanco to cost-controlled, long-term extensions and made a pair of shrewd trades that brought Joe Ryan for Cruz in 2021 and Pablo López for Luis Arraez in 2023.
But even with the good moves, Falvey wasn’t at his best when he spent money. The 2018 offseason was a disaster as Falvey signed Lance Lynn, Logan Morrison and Addison Reed to a combined $35.25 million. In 2020, he signed Josh Donaldson to a four-year, $92 million contract. In 2021, he signed Alex Colomé to a one-year, $6.25 million contract to watch him post a 4.15 ERA and after wisely signing Carlos Correa in 2022, he handed out a six-year, $200 million contract the following offseason after the Mets and the San Francisco Giants backed out of mega-deals over long-term health concerns.
These contracts emphasized some of the other poor decisions Falvey made over the years. While Hunter Greene has had arm problems this season, his performance during the 2024 and 2025 seasons (16-9, 2.76 ERA) suggests he would have been a better choice than Royce Lewis with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 MLB Draft.
The 2022 trade deadline was another disaster as Falvey traded for Tyler Mahle and Jorge López only to have both pitchers flame out within a calendar year. The trade for Chris Paddack before the 2022 season sent out a future All-Star in Brent Rooker and the Twins only won one playoff series during his nine seasons with the team.
The Twins left the Mets a warning about Derek Falvey
Falvey’s overall resume is likely what’s appealing to the Mets and they could use some new voices after a disappointing year. After spending $359.2 million in payroll this season per Cot’s Baseball Contracts, New York is currently last in the National League East with a 73-85 record. Their roster is filled with contracts that would make Falvey blush from his time with the Twins. But if they’re expecting him to solve their issues, they should look at the mess he left behind in Minnesota.
The Twins lineup is filled with players that Falvey drafted but never reached their potential. Lewis is the headliner, but others such as Trevor Larnach and Matt Wallner have turned out to be below-average players with Wallner still stuck in the minor leagues.
Falvey’s final free agent signings also didn’t turn out well. While Josh Bell had a solid season, hitting .255/.317/.416 with 20 homers and 92 RBI, Victor Caratini looks like a similar mistake to Christian Vazquez’s three-year, $30 million contract in 2023.
The lack of starting pitching, something that was regarded as a calling card for Falvey coming over from the Guardians, was also glaring as the Twins scrambled to fill roles with Zebby Matthews and Connor Prielipp.
Even one of Falvey’s worst trades as general manager haunted this year’s team as Austin Martin posted an OPS+ of 88 (100 is league average) and Simeon Woods Richardson didn’t make it to June after being acquired in the 2022 trade that sent Jose Berríos to the Toronto Blue Jays.
With that, bringing in Falvey to try and solve the issues the Mets have feels a lot like his promotion to the president of baseball and business operations ahead of the 2025 season. Falvey won’t have as much power in New York, but it also could dispel the theory that giving him some more money to throw at his problems won’t magically turn him into a competent executive.

SAN FRANCISCO — Before the regular season concludes on Sunday, manager Tony Vitello has one last piece of business to address.
The Giants have already used 70 different players this season, surpassing the previous franchise record (66) set under former president of baseball operations Farhan Zaidi. With three games remaining, a weekend homestand against the Dodgers that begins Friday night, Vitello has one more player who needs to see the field before it’s all said and done.
Zach Morgan, who grew up in Stockton as a Giants fan, spent eight games on San Francisco’s roster this season but has yet to debut. The 26-year-old catcher rejoined the team on the taxi squad on Wednesday after Osleivis Basabe’s hamstring flared up the previous day. Vitello said he is going to find a way to get him into a game.
“Come hell or high water, I’d like to get him on that field and give him an opportunity to do something,” Vitello said.
If and when Morgan makes his major-league debut, the Giants will tie the 2025 Atlanta Braves for the most players used in a single season. When Vitello was asked about using so many players before Wednesday’s 4-2 loss to the Minnesota Twins, the first-year manager at least had a sense of humor.
“I guess being first year in the organization, you’d like to get to meet everybody,” Vitello said. “So, this is one way to do it.”
Given the amount of established regulars on the Opening Day roster, the Giants could never have envisioned needing so many players to get through one of the worst and weirdest seasons in franchise history. It’s a dizzying roster churn that’s largely been the product of an absolutely ruthless injury bug.
Since last Friday, San Francisco has placed four players — Logan Webb, Bryce Eldridge, Jung Hoo Lee and Blade Tidwell — on the injured list. Eldridge landed in concussion protocol after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles last week, while Lee sustained a groin contusion after fouling a ball off a sensitive area.
As for Tidwell, he’s likely headed for surgery after being diagnosed with a “high-grade” UCL sprain and could miss the entire 2027 season. Tidwell will become the Giants’ fourth young starter to undergo a UCL procedure this year, joining Hayden Birdsong, Trevor McDonald and Carson Whisenhunt.
Since August, Casey Schmitt (torn meniscus), Matt Chapman (core), Rafael Devers (core) and Daniel Susac (patella fracture) have undergone season-ending surgery. Willy Adames didn’t go under the knife, but the left elbow sprain he sustained in late August ended up ending his season.
There’s also Harrison Bader, who played just 30 games after sustaining multiple injuries, then crashing into a fire truck while riding a scooter in the wee hours of the morning.
The Giants currently have 16 players on the 60-day injured list, and according to FanGraphs’ Jon Becker, the last team with that many players on their 60-day IL was the 2021 Texas Rangers. San Francisco’s brass will have many cuts to make in the offseason, especially with prospects such as Henry Lalane and Marty Gair eligible for the Rule 5 Draft (which may not happen due to the impending lockout).
Among those on the Opening Day roster, only infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp remain, the latter of whom was shut down for the rest of the season.
“Odd is a good word,” Koss said. “I would have to look up how many times it’s happened in a baseball season. I imagine it’s pretty low. It’s kind of one of those things we’ve had to deal with this season.”
Injuries aren’t the only reason why the Giants have called on so many different names.
Seven members of the Opening Day roster – Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez, Robbie Ray, Erik Miller, Tyler Mahle, Caleb Kilian — were shipped to other teams this season. Bailey was shockingly traded to the Cleveland Guardians in May, but the rest of the bunch was dealt right before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
The abnormal roster churn has led to its share of odd facts and figures.
San Francisco has also had a franchise-record 17 players make their MLB debuts, the latest being outfielder Bo Davidson. Vitello has also used 15 different leadoff hitters, tied for the most used by a single team in MLB history (since at least 1898).
The Giants have had six different players homer while playing catcher this season which, per Sarah Langs, is tied with the 2022 Reds and 2019 A’s for the most in a single season. Five players — César Perdomo (No. 83), Seth Lonsway (No. 86), Braxton Roxby (No. 90), Scott Bandura (No. 91) and Davidson (No. 94) — have worn numbers that have never previously been used in franchise history.
For Vitello, if there is any semblance of a silver lining, it’s that he’s experienced “so many cool moments and be a part of kids’ lives.” On Wednesday, Vitello recalled seeing video of Davidson’s family celebrate his first career hit, a single to cap off a nine-pitch at-bat.
“That’s been a huge bright spot on a year where there’s been a lot of days — full transparency — back in the locker room that aren’t too pretty,” Vitello said.

DENVER (AP) — Corbin Carroll had a two-run triple to cap a four-run first inning and the Arizona Diamondbacks kept their playoff hopes alive with a 5-3 victory over the Colorado Rockies on Wednesday night.
Gabriel Moreno drove in the first run and finished with three hits to help Arizona (84-74) close within three games of the Phillies and Cubs for an NL wild card.
Moreno, with a .310 batting average, trails the Phillies’ Luis Arraez at .312 for the NL batting title with four games remaining.
Merrill Kelly (10-14) allowed two runs over 5 1/3 innings to improve to 6-0 in nine starts at Coors Field since 2022. Jonathan Loáisiga earned his second save when he retired Ezequiel Tovar on a foul pop that first baseman Ildemaro Vargas caught at the railing with runners on second and third.
Ketel Marte reached second when Zac Veen misplayed his one-out liner to left field in the first and Moreno singled off rookie Mason Adams (0-2) two pitches later for the lead.
Nolan Arenado added an RBI single before Carroll hit his 17th triple — the most in the majors this season. The Rockies have allowed an MLB-high 131 first-inning runs.
Adams retired 13 straight following Carroll’s triple until Moreno singled leading off the sixth. All four runs off the right-hander were unearned. He allowed five hits and struck out eight in six innings for the first time in his six starts.
Adael Amador had an RBI double in the second and Hunter Goodman added a sacrifice fly in the third for the Rockies (57-101).
Tim Tawa hit his 11th homer off Mark Manfredi for a 5-2 lead in the eighth.
Tovar answered with his 12th home run of the season off Brandyn Garcia in the bottom of the inning.

Yordan Alvarez, Jacob Misiorowski, AL, NL Stat Leaders Ahead of 2026 MLB Season's Final Weekend
With five days remaining in the 2026 MLB regular season, the individual stats leaderboard is almost as unsettled as the playoff races in both leagues.
The key races going into the final weekend involve Yordan Alvarez's quest for the AL triple crown and Jacob Misiorowski looking to lead all of MLB in strikeouts.
Here are the leaders in several individual categories going into Wednesday's games.

| Category | American League | National League |
| Batting Average | Yordan Alvarez (Astros): .314 | Luis Arraez (Phillies): .314 |
| Home Runs | Alvarez (Astros) and Junior Caminero (Rays): 41 | Kyle Schwarber (Phillies) and Pete Crow-Armstrong (Cubs): 45 |
| RBI | Pete Alonso (Orioles): 108 | Alec Burleson (Cardinals): 111 |
| Hits | Yandy Diaz (Rays): 175 | Otto Lopez (Marlins): 186 |
| Stolen Bases | Chandler Simpson (Rays): 46 | Nasim Nunez (Nationals): 47 |
| Wins | Sonny Gray (Red Sox): 17 | Cristopher Sánchez (Phillies): 18 |
| Innings | Michael Wacha (Royals): 194.1 | Sandy Alcantara (Marlins): 212.0 |
| ERA | Cam Schlittler (Yankees): 1.94 | Jacob Misiorowski (Brewers): 1.86 |
| Strikeouts | Gavin Williams (Guardians): 244 | Jacob Misiorowski (Brewers): 247 |
| Saves | Bryan Baker (Rays) and Cade Smith (Guardians): 40 | Riley O'Brien (Cardinals): 38 |
Alvarez will need a strong close to the season to win the triple crown. He still leads the AL in average and is tied for the lead in homers, but his RBI pace has fallen off this month.
The Houston Astros star had just five RBI in his first 16 games in September before driving in three on Tuesday in a 7-0 win over the Seattle Mariners.
Alvarez is up to 102 RBI for the season. Pete Alonso's 17 RBI this month have pushed him up to 108 with five games remaining.
Alvarez and Luis Arraez are tied for the MLB lead with a .314 batting average. Both players look like safe bets to maintain that position through Sunday.
Misiorowski, the biggest breakout star of the season for the 2026 NL Central champion Milwaukee Brewers, is looking to become the first pitcher to lead MLB in both ERA and strikeouts in a 162-game season since Jake Peavy in 2007.
The MLB ERA title is down to Misiorowski at 1.86 and New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler at 1.94. Misiorowski will likely get one more abbreviated start in Milwaukee's final regular-season series against the St. Louis Cardinals.
Schlittler is scheduled to make his final regular-season start on Thursday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Since the Yankees are locked into the No. 4 seed, he is also likely to have a shortened outing to prepare for Game 1 of the wild-card round on Tuesday.
The strikeout race is arguably more compelling than the ERA title because Gavin Williams of the Cleveland Guardians will likely get the nod on Friday against the Kansas City Royals.
Since the Guardians can't wrap up the AL Central until Friday at the earliest, Williams will likely have a regular outing. He is currently only three Ks behind Misiorowski for the MLB lead.
Williams has 15 strikeouts in 11.2 innings against the Royals this season, but he hasn't faced them since May 5.
NL MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong is one stolen base away from the seventh player in MLB history to have a 40-40 season. He can also become the first Chicago Cubs player to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa hit 49 in 2002.

SEATTLE (AP) — Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez gained some ground Tuesday night in his chase for a Triple Crown.
He still has plenty of work to do this week.
The AL MVP front-runner went 2 for 4 with his 41st home run and three RBIs in the Astros' 7-0 win over the Seattle Mariners. Alvarez hit an RBI single in the first inning, was intentionally walked in the second and then belted a 386-foot homer in the eighth with a 109.5 mph exit velocity.
“At this point, I keep wondering why guys are pitching to him,” Houston first baseman Christian Walker said. “He just seems to come through in every moment. He's dangerous at the plate right now.”
Alvarez, who is quiet and shows little emotion, orchestrated a team meeting after the Astros (78-79) were swept by Atlanta on Sunday, squandering their lead in the AL West. His performance on Tuesday was much-needed to put Houston in a tie with the Texas Rangers atop the division with five games left this season.
“He's been backing it up all year,” Astros manager Joe Espada said.
Alvarez's two-run shot to right field tied him with Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays for the American League lead with 41 homers. Alvarez is first in batting average at .314 — five points ahead of Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson — and he has 102 RBIs, six behind Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso for most in the AL.
Alonso drove in three runs with two homers Monday against Toronto, but the teams were rained out Tuesday in Baltimore because of bad weather. They are scheduled to play a split doubleheader Wednesday.
Alvarez has six homers since Aug. 1, and the 29-year-old designated hitter has eight RBIs over 17 games in September. He'll need more to become baseball’s first Triple Crown winner since Miguel Cabrera in 2012.
Alvarez leads the AL in slugging percentage (.601), OPS (1.032), total bases (329) and walks (106). Logan Gilbert intentionally walked Alvarez in the second inning Tuesday, which was the 33rd time for Alvarez this season, already a franchise record.
It’s been a historic season for the four-time All-Star after he was limited to 48 games in 2025 because of a broken hand and an ankle injury.
If he wins the AL MVP award, the Cuban slugger will join Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers as the only players to win an MVP award while primarily serving as a designated hitter. Othani was close to winning a Triple Crown in 2024 after leading the NL in homers (50) and RBIs (130), but his .310 average fell just short to Luis Arráez’s .314.

The San Francisco Giants are going into a rebuild after trading away several top names at the MLB Trade Deadline, such as Luis Arraez, Heliot Ramos, and Robbie Ray. But with every rebuild, there's always a possibility for a familiar face to get a second chance with the franchise, depending on specific needs.
It's clear the Giants bullpen is one of those specific needs, holding a bullpen ERA of 4.18 and only collecting 30 saves this season. With many young pitchers looking to pave their path into the bullpen, this club needs a veteran reliever that it can rely on.
Across the league, the Pittsburgh Pirates announced Tuesday afternoon that they've designated former San Francisco Giants closer Camilo Doval for assignment as a corresponding move to activate Kirby Yates off the injured list.
Isn't that crazy how the world of baseball works? Doval spent his best years as a member of the Giants organization, holding a 3.29 ERA in 275 games for the franchise from 2021 to 2025, when he was traded to the New York Yankees. As a Giant, Doval collected 107 saves. Elsewhere, between the Yankees and the Pirates, Doval has recorded two saves.
Should the Giants Reunite with Doval?
This season, Doval holds a 4.30 ERA and a 1.52 WHIP with New York and Pittsburgh, having pitched well with the Pirates, but not well enough for the team to keep him around. Pirates manager Don Kelly had a blunt statement about Doval that the Giants know well.
“He had some really good games and a couple tough ones,” Kelly said via Aiden Stepansky of MLB.com. “He's got some really good stuff, and ultimately, it really just came down to being able to maximize innings.
It's not like Doval has lost all of what made him an All-Star in 2023, but he hasn't been that pitcher since. However, having tested the waters away from San Francisco, and then the Giants testing the waters without Doval, perhaps it's a reunion that has to happen.
Doval seemed to have figured it out the first month he was in Pittsburgh, pitching to a 2.84 ERA in August. But in September, it's been a different story, in which he's posted a 5.68 ERA in 6.1 innings across seven games.
Bringing Doval back to a franchise where he has previously felt comfortable and confident could be beneficial. As a veteran closer, he has the opportunity to mentor the younger players, while learning from them as well. San Francisco might be making the right choice by following the path that seems laid out before them.
According to MLB's DFA rules, within seven days of the transaction, the player can either be traded or placed on outright or unconditional release waivers. So, the Giants could be a team to watch for the next few days to see if they're a fit for their former reliever again.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.
